c: int *b = a;               /* b is an ALIAS: same block, not a copy */
printf("a and b point to the same block: %s\n", (a == b) ? "true" : "false");
*b = 99;                  /* writing through b is visible through a too */
/* Correct order: free the block through one of the aliases, THEN clear both. */
b = NULL;                 /* free() does not clear pointers for you -- we must */
printf("freed and cleared: a = %p, b = %p\n", (void *) a, (void *) b);
java: Counter b = a;              // b is an ALIAS: same object, not a copy
System.out.println("a and b refer to the same object: " + (a == b));
b.value = 99;                // changing through b is visible through a too
a = null;                    // one reference gone; still reachable through b
b = null;                    // last reference gone: now eligible for GC
System.out.println("b = " + b + " (the Counter object has no reachable reference left)");

cap.en: `b = null;` -- the last reference is gone too. There is now NO way to reach the object: it becomes a candidate for the garbage collector.

cap.tr: Java'da hiçbir zaman `free()` çağırmadık; çöp toplayıcı erişilemeyen nesneleri kendi zamanında temizler. C sekmesine bakın: orada aynı senaryoyu ELLE yönetmek gerekir -- `free` edip HER İKİ takma adı da NULL yapmazsanız, blok sonsuza dek sızar (leak), ama asla çökmez de.
cap.en: We never called `free()` in Java; the garbage collector sweeps unreachable objects on its own schedule. Check the C tab: there, the same scenario must be managed BY HAND -- free it and NULL out BOTH aliases, or the block leaks forever without ever crashing.
